title: Jackson v. Southfield Neighborhood Revitalization Initiative
description: Whether a governmental unit commits a taking under the Michigan Constitution when it acquires tax-foreclosed properties for the minimum bid through a right-of-first-refusal process without a public auction, and whether subsequent statutory amendments apply retroactively.
plaintiff_argument: The governmental units violated their constitutional rights, including the Takings Clauses, by retaining surplus value from their foreclosed properties without just compensation, and amended MCL 211.78m should apply retroactively.
defendant_argument: The trial court lacked jurisdiction, plaintiffs lacked standing, the suit was barred by res judicata, Rafaeli did not apply retroactively, plaintiffs had no protected property interests, and amended MCL 211.78m does not apply retroactively.
decision_outcome: The court held that a taking occurs when a governmental unit obtains surplus value from tax-foreclosed properties acquired for the minimum bid without public auction, that MCL 211.78t applies retroactively but not to this case, and that amended MCL 211.78m applies prospectively only, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Michigan Immigrant Rights Center v. Governor
description: Whether the Court of Claims Act's one-year notice provision applies to claims seeking prospective relief against state officers for alleged state and federal constitutional violations.
plaintiff_argument: The notice provision of the Court of Claims Act does not apply to claims for prospective relief against state officers, especially for constitutional claims, as it only applies to claims based on past harms, not future harms.
defendant_argument: The notice provision of the Court of Claims Act does apply to the plaintiff's suit, and the plaintiff failed to comply with it by not filing notice within one year of the claim accruing.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court denied the plaintiff's application for leave to appeal, thereby upholding the Court of Appeals' decision that the notice provision of the Court of Claims Act applies to the plaintiff's suit for prospective relief, leading to the dismissal of the case.

title: People v. Armstrong
description: Whether the Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (MRTMA) superseded the rule that the smell of marijuana alone establishes probable cause to search a motor vehicle under the warrant exception, with the prosecution arguing it does not and the defendant arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the smell of marijuana alone provided sufficient probable cause to search the vehicle under prior precedent (Kazmierczak) or that the gun was observed in plain view during a lawful investigatory stop.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the gun was discovered during an unlawful search that violated the Fourth Amendment, as the smell of marijuana alone no longer constitutes probable cause after the decriminalization of marijuana.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision to suppress the evidence (the gun) and dismiss the charges against the defendant, ruling that the smell of marijuana alone is no longer sufficient to establish probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search.

title: People v. Taylor; People v. Czarnecki
description: Whether mandatorily subjecting 19- and 20-year-old defendants convicted of first-degree murder to a sentence of life without parole (LWOP) violates Michigan's constitutional prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The mandatory LWOP sentence for 19- and 20-year-olds is constitutional, as the Legislature's judgment on severe crimes should be respected, and Michigan's sentencing scheme is not an outlier compared to other jurisdictions.
defendant_argument: The mandatory LWOP sentence for 19- and 20-year-olds is unconstitutional because it is disproportionate, fails to consider youth-related mitigating factors due to late-adolescent brain development, and prevents rehabilitation, violating Michigan's cruel or unusual punishment clause.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacated the defendants' mandatory LWOP sentences for first-degree murder, and remanded the cases for individualized resentencing, extending the protections previously granted to 18-year-olds to 19- and 20-year-old offenders.

title: Heos v. City of East Lansing
description: Whether the franchise fee imposed by the City of East Lansing on electric utility consumers, collected by the Lansing Board of Water and Light (LBWL), constitutes an unlawful tax requiring voter approval under the Headlee Amendment, or a legitimate user fee.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the franchise fee is an illegal tax violating the Headlee Amendment and other state laws because it was not approved by voters, and that he is a taxpayer with a timely claim.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the franchise fee is a legitimate user fee, or alternatively, that the plaintiff is not a "taxpayer" but a "member of the public," making his Headlee Amendment claims time-barred.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, ruling that the franchise fee is an unauthorized tax violating the Headlee Amendment and that the plaintiff is a taxpayer with a viable claim, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: People v. Poole
description: Whether People v Parks, which held that mandatory life-without-parole sentences for 18-year-old homicide offenders violated the Michigan Constitution, applies retroactively to cases where the period for direct review had expired when Parks was decided. The prosecution argued it should not apply retroactively, while the defendant argued it should.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the Court of Appeals erred by concluding that Parks applied retroactively.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Parks applied retroactively, entitling him to resentencing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court held that the Parks ruling, which found mandatory life-without-parole sentences for 18-year-old homicide offenders unconstitutional, applies retroactively, affirming the Court of Appeals' decision to vacate the defendant's sentence and remand for resentencing.

title: People v. Loew
description: Whether ex parte communications between a trial judge and the prosecutor warrant granting the defendant a new trial under MCR 6.431(B), with the plaintiff arguing such communications were harmless and the defendant arguing they violated his due process rights and created an appearance of impropriety.
plaintiff_argument: The ex parte communications were for administrative purposes, did not show actual bias, did not affect the jury, and did not violate the defendant's constitutional rights, therefore a new trial is not warranted.
defendant_argument: The trial judge's ex parte communications with the prosecutor violated judicial conduct, created an appearance of impropriety, and deprived him of his constitutional rights to a fair trial, to be present, and to counsel, thus warranting a new trial.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, which had reversed the trial court's grant of a new trial, thereby denying the defendant a new trial.

title: O’Halloran v. Sec. of State
description: Whether the Secretary of State's 2022 election manual provisions regarding challenger credentials, challenger liaisons, permissible challenges, and electronic devices are consistent with Michigan Election Law or require formal promulgation under the Administrative Procedures Act (APA).
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the challenged provisions in the 2022 manual either conflicted with the Michigan Election Law or constituted administrative rules that needed to be promulgated through the formal process outlined in the Administrative Procedures Act (APA).
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the challenged provisions were lawful, consistent with Michigan Election Law, and fell within exceptions to APA rulemaking as interpretive statements or forms with instructions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated in part, finding the electronic device ban moot, upholding the uniform credential form and most challenger liaison and challenge categorization provisions, but striking down parts that gave liaisons arbitrary discretion.

title: People v. Neilly
description: Whether the trial court violated federal and state constitutional prohibitions on ex post facto laws by ordering defendant to pay restitution under current statutes during resentencing, rather than the statutes in effect at the time of his crimes.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that restitution under current statutes is a civil remedy, not a criminal punishment, and therefore its application does not violate ex post facto prohibitions.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that applying current restitution statutes, which are more stringent than those in effect at the time of his crime, retroactively increased his punishment in violation of ex post facto clauses.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's order, holding that restitution under current statutes is a civil remedy and does not violate ex post facto prohibitions.

title: People v. Lymon
description: Whether requiring a defendant to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offenders Registration Act (SORA) for a non-sexual crime, such as unlawful imprisonment of a minor, constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution or the US Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that SORA registration for non-sexual offenders is a reasonable measure for public protection, consistent with legislative intent and practices in many other states, and does not constitute cruel or unusual punishment.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that requiring registration as a sex offender for a non-sexual crime constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution, as sex offender registries do not effectively reduce recidivism and impose excessive burdens and stigma.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the imposition of the 2021 SORA on non-sexual offenders constitutes cruel or unusual punishment under the Michigan Constitution and affirmed the judgment to remove such offenders from the sex-offender registry.

title: Mothering Justice v. Attorney General
description: Whether the Michigan Legislature can adopt an initiative petition and then amend it in the same legislative session, given the constitutional provisions for direct democracy.
plaintiff_argument: The Legislature's 'adopt-and-amend' practice is unconstitutional under Article 2, § 9 of the Michigan Constitution, which outlines only three options for handling initiative petitions, none of which permit adopting and then amending in the same session.
defendant_argument: The Michigan Constitution does not expressly prohibit the Legislature from adopting and amending an initiative proposal in the same legislative session, and therefore, the Legislature is free to do so under its general legislative power.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, declared 2018 PA 368 and 2018 PA 369 unconstitutional, and ordered 2018 PA 337 and 2018 PA 338 to go into effect 205 days after July 31, 2024, with a revised schedule for minimum wage increases and inflation adjustments.

title: Planned Parenthood of Michigan v. Attorney General of the State of Michigan
description: Whether MCL 750.14, which prohibits all abortions except those performed to preserve the life of a woman, violates the Michigan Constitution's Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses.
plaintiff_argument: MCL 750.14 violates the Due Process, Equal Protection, and Retained Rights provisions of the Michigan Constitution, and the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, by infringing on the fundamental right to bodily integrity and privacy, and creating an illegal sex-based classification.
defendant_argument: MCL 750.14 is constitutional, arguing that Michigan's Due Process Clause does not include a right to abortion, the right to bodily integrity does not encompass abortion, and the law does not create a sex-based classification subject to heightened scrutiny.
decision_outcome: The Court declares MCL 750.14 unconstitutional on its face and permanently enjoins the Attorney General of the State of Michigan from enforcing it.

title: People v. Posey
description: Whether due-process rights are violated by first-time in-court identifications and whether within-guidelines sentences are subject to appellate review for reasonableness.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the in-court identification was admissible and reliable, or that any error was not prejudicial, and that within-guidelines sentences should be affirmed as per MCL 769.34(10).
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his due process rights were violated by the first-time in-court identification and that MCL 769.34(10) unconstitutionally precluded appellate review of his within-guidelines sentence.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the defendant's conviction but reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment regarding sentencing, remanding the case for a reasonableness review of the defendant's sentence.

title: Mt. Clemens Recreational Bowl v. Director of the Department of Health & Human Services
description: Whether the state's COVID-19 shutdown orders constituted an unconstitutional taking of private property or actionable torts, and whether the case should have been transferred to a circuit court for a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the COVID-19 shutdown orders constituted a compensable regulatory taking of their property, that they had actionable tort claims, and that they had a right to a jury trial in circuit court, necessitating a transfer from the Court of Claims.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Court of Claims had exclusive jurisdiction, the shutdown orders were a valid exercise of police power and not a compensable taking, and governmental immunity protected them from tort claims as the Governor's actions were not ultra vires.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's decision, denying the plaintiffs' motion to transfer and granting summary disposition to the defendants on all claims.

title: The Gym 24/7 Fitness LLC v. State of Michigan
description: Whether a business owner is entitled to just compensation under the Takings Clause when the government temporarily closes their business using police power to protect public health during a pandemic.
plaintiff_argument: The Gym argued that even if the Governor's executive orders were a proper exercise of police power for a public purpose, the state and federal constitutions require "just compensation" for the temporary taking of its business operations and revenues.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the proper exercise of police power to protect public health and safety during an epidemic does not constitute a compensable taking, and therefore, no compensation is owed for temporary public health measures.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Court of Claims' decision and ruled in favor of the State, holding that the temporary closure of businesses under executive orders during a pandemic does not constitute a compensable taking under the state or federal constitutions.

title: People v. Johnson
description: Whether MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii), which allows trial courts to assess operational costs on convicted defendants, violates separation of powers and due process principles.
plaintiff_argument: The statute is constitutional and does not violate separation of powers or due process, as previously upheld by the Court of Appeals.
defendant_argument: The statute is unconstitutional, violating separation of powers by assigning legislative taxation duties to the judiciary and due process by creating a potential for judicial bias.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated its prior order granting leave to appeal and denied the defendant's application for leave to appeal, thereby upholding the lower court's decision that the statute is constitutional.

title: People v. Edwards
description: Whether MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii), which allows courts to impose costs to fund their operations, violates separation-of-powers and due process principles by creating a potential for judicial bias, with the defendant arguing it is unconstitutional and the plaintiff arguing it is constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argues that MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii) is constitutional, does not create an unconstitutional potential for bias, and that no actual bias has been demonstrated by judges.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that MCL 769.1k(1)(b)(iii) violates separation-of-powers and due process by creating a pecuniary interest for judges in the outcome of criminal cases, thus creating a potential for bias.
decision_outcome: The Court vacated its prior order granting leave to appeal and denied the application for leave to appeal, stating it was no longer persuaded that the questions presented should be reviewed.

title: Reproductive Freedom for All v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether a constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature under Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1, must be limited to a single purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The proposed amendment must be limited to a single purpose and fails this test because it addresses both term limits and financial disclosures.
defendant_argument: The text of Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 does not establish a single-purpose test for amendments proposed by the Legislature.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the plaintiffs' complaint for mandamus and declaratory relief.

title: Promote The Vote 2022 v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether the Board of State Canvassers has a clear legal duty to certify the Promote the Vote petition for the ballot, given challenges that it fails to republish abrogated constitutional provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the proposed amendments would not abrogate any existing constitutional provisions and that the petition met all formal and signature requirements, thus the Board had a clear legal duty to certify it.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Defend Your Vote) argued that the petition failed to include all constitutional provisions that would be abrogated by the proposed amendments, as required by law, and therefore the Board had a clear legal duty to withhold certification.
decision_outcome: The court granted the complaint for mandamus and declaratory relief, ordering the Board of State Canvassers to certify the Promote the Vote petition for placement on the November 8 general election ballot.

title: Anderson v. Board of State Canvassers
description: Whether a constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature under Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 must be limited to a single purpose.
plaintiff_argument: The constitutional amendment proposed by the Legislature must be limited to a single purpose, and the current amendment (term limits and financial disclosures) fails this test as it has two purposes.
defendant_argument: The text of Const. 1963, art. 12, § 1 does not establish a single-purpose test for legislative-proposed amendments.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the requested relief, finding it was not persuaded to grant it.

title: People v. Boykin
description: Whether trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when sentencing them to a term of years, and whether this consideration must be articulated on the record.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that trial courts are not required to consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor or articulate it on the record when imposing a term-of-years sentence, as Miller v Alabama only applies to life-without-parole sentences.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when imposing a term-of-years sentence, and that failure to do so or articulate it on the record violates constitutional principles.
decision_outcome: The court held that trial courts must consider a juvenile offender's youth as a mitigating factor when sentencing them to term-of-years sentences, but this consideration need not be articulated on the record. The Court vacated the Court of Appeals judgments regarding sentencing challenges and remanded both cases for further consideration.

title: People v. Parks
description: Whether mandatory life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for 18-year-old homicide offenders violates the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution or the Michigan Constitution's prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that mandatory life without parole for 18-year-old offenders is constitutional and that Miller's protections should not be extended to this age group.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that mandatory life without parole for 18-year-old offenders constitutes cruel and/or unusual punishment under both the federal and state Constitutions, seeking to extend Miller's protections.
decision_outcome: The court held that mandatorily subjecting 18-year-old defendants convicted of first-degree murder to a sentence of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole violates the principle of proportionality derived from the Michigan Constitution, constituting unconstitutionally cruel punishment, and remanded the case for resentencing.

title: People v. Stovall
description: Whether a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole for a defendant who committed second-degree murder while a juvenile constitutes cruel or unusual punishment and therefore violates Const 1963, art 1, § 16.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the defendant's parolable life sentences were constitutionally proportionate and that his motion for relief from judgment was procedurally barred.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his parolable life sentences for second-degree murder, committed as a juvenile, violated the Michigan Constitution's prohibition against cruel or unusual punishment, and that his plea bargain was illusory.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the defendant's sentence for second-degree murder, ruling that it violates Article 1, § 16 of the Michigan Constitution, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Bauserman v. Unemployment Insurance Agency
description: Whether plaintiffs have alleged a cognizable state constitutional-tort claim allowing them to recover a judicially inferred damages remedy for due process violations.
plaintiff_argument: Plaintiffs argue that the Unemployment Insurance Agency violated their due-process rights by using an automated fraud-detection system to seize property and impose penalties without adequate notice or opportunity to be heard, and they seek monetary damages for this constitutional tort.
defendant_argument: Defendant argues that plaintiffs' claims were not timely filed, that alternative remedies existed under the Michigan Employment Security Act, and that creating a constitutional-tort claim for monetary damages is beyond the court's authority and falls to the Legislature.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's denial of summary disposition for the defendant, ruling that plaintiffs have a cognizable constitutional-tort claim for monetary damages for due process violations, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Detroit Caucus v. Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the adopted redistricting plans violate federal laws, specifically the Voting Rights Act of 1965, by unlawfully diluting the voting power of minority groups.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that the absence of an equivalent number of majority-minority districts in the adopted plans, compared to existing districts, constitutes unlawful vote dilution in violation of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that the adopted plans comply with federal law and the VRA, as there was no strong basis in evidence to believe the Gingles preconditions for requiring race-based districts were met, and that white crossover voting ensures equal opportunity.
decision_outcome: The Court denied the relief requested and dismissed the first amended verified complaint, ruling that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the Commission's adopted plans are noncompliant with federal law.

title: League of Women Voters of Michigan v. Secretary of State
description: Whether 2018 PA 608's 15% geographic distribution requirement, paid circulator affidavit requirement, and circulator checkbox requirement for petition circulation are constitutional, with plaintiffs arguing they are unconstitutional burdens on direct democracy and defendants arguing they are constitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the 15% geographic distribution requirement, the paid circulator affidavit requirement, and the circulator checkbox requirement imposed by 2018 PA 608 were unconstitutional burdens on direct democracy and free speech rights.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the challenged provisions of 2018 PA 608 were constitutional and did not unduly burden direct democracy or free speech rights.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the 15% geographic distribution requirement and the paid circulator affidavit requirement were unconstitutional, but the checkbox requirement was constitutional, and the decision would apply prospectively only.

title: The Detroit News,  Inc. v. Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission's attorney-client communications and work product, including a closed-session meeting recording and ten memoranda, are subject to public disclosure under constitutional transparency requirements, with plaintiffs arguing for disclosure and the Commission arguing for privilege.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, a group of news organizations, sought the production of a recording from the Commission's closed-session meeting and disclosure of ten memoranda, contending that these materials constitute 'business' and 'supporting materials' that must be public under constitutional transparency mandates.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Independent Citizens Redistricting Commission, asserted that the meeting and memoranda were privileged attorney-client communications, arguing that 'supporting materials' should be limited to factual information, not legal opinions, and that the meeting was related to inevitable litigation.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Commission's October 27 closed-session meeting violated the constitutional requirement to conduct all business at open meetings, and ordered the disclosure of the meeting recording. The court also ordered the publication of seven of the ten memoranda as 'supporting materials' used to develop redistricting plans, but found the remaining three were not 'supporting materials' and need not be disclosed.

title: Sheffield v. Detroit City Clerk
description: Whether the Detroit Charter Revision Commission may submit a proposed revised charter to voters without the Governor's approval.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that MCL 117.22 requires gubernatorial approval for a revised charter to be submitted to voters.
defendant_argument: The Detroit Charter Revision Commission argued that MCL 117.22's silence on gubernatorial approval means it can submit the revised charter to voters without the Governor's signature.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' judgments, allowing the Detroit Charter Revision Commission to submit the proposed revised charter to voters without the Governor's approval.

title: People v. Washington
description: Whether the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced defendant in 2006 while defendant's application for leave to appeal that order was still pending in the Supreme Court.
plaintiff_argument: The prosecution argued that the trial court did not lack subject-matter jurisdiction and that the defendant's successive motion for relief from judgment was barred by court rules.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when it resentenced him in 2006 because his application for leave to appeal was still pending before the Michigan Supreme Court.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the trial court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction in 2006, rendering the resentencing void, and remanded for resentencing consistent with the 2016 order.

title: Taxpayers for Michigan Constitutional Government v. State
description: Whether certain state funds, specifically Proposal A payments to school districts, state spending for state-mandated local services, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs), should be included in the calculation of "total state spending paid to all units of Local Government" under § 30 of the Headlee Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Proposal A payments, state spending for state-mandated local services, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs) should not be counted as part of total state spending paid to local governments, as their inclusion improperly inflates the figure and shortchanges local governments.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that Proposal A payments, state spending for state-mandated local services, and state aid to Public School Academies (PSAs) are properly counted as part of total state spending paid to local governments, as these funds are collected and disbursed by the state to units of local government.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed that Proposal A payments and state-mandated local services spending are properly counted, reversed the Court of Appeals' conclusion that PSAs are "school districts" and are not political subdivisions of the state, and remanded the issue of PSA funding and mandamus relief to the Court of Appeals for further consideration.

title: People v. Pagano
description: Whether an anonymous 911 tip, without independent corroboration of criminal activity, provides sufficient reasonable and articulable suspicion for a police officer to conduct an investigatory traffic stop under the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the anonymous 911 tip, which included identifying details of the vehicle and allegations of intoxication, provided sufficient reasonable and articulable suspicion for the investigatory stop.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the anonymous tip, lacking independent corroboration of criminal activity, did not provide the police officer with reasonable and articulable suspicion, thus violating the Fourth Amendment.
decision_outcome: The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the investigatory stop violated the Fourth Amendment because the police officer lacked reasonable and articulable suspicion of criminal activity.
